temple_mater_matuta_v1.note: Conventional attribution: temple B (east), its cella under the church of Sant'Omobono, = Mater Matuta; temple A (west, fully visible) = Fortuna. No inscription fixes which is which. Podium height includes the raised platform.

temple_fortuna_v1.note: Conventional attribution: temple A (west, fully visible) = Fortuna; temple B (east, under the church) = Mater Matuta. Podium height includes the raised platform.

santomobono_archaic_temple.note: Found in deep soundings under the apse of the church of Sant'Omobono (area of the later eastern temple B, Mater Matuta), on a slightly different orientation from the twin temples.

castra_praetoria_v1.note: Rectangle 440 x 380 m (sides along 340/160 and 70/250, from the Aurelian Wall which follows its N, E and S sides). rot 250 = side facing the city (WSW); the porta praetoria was in the NNW side and the porta principalis dextera in the E side (OSM nodes).

circus_varianus_v1.note: Carceres at the Aurelian Wall c. 12.5175, 41.8880 (OSM 'Carceres del Circo Variano'); curved end at Via Alcamo (c. 12.5239, 41.8863); N side under the Acqua Felice. Axis c. 110/290; 565 m after Elagabalus shortened it (originally c. 630 m).

circus_varianus_v2.note: Carceres at the Aurelian Wall c. 12.5175, 41.8880 (OSM 'Carceres del Circo Variano'); curved end at Via Alcamo (c. 12.5239, 41.8863); N side under the Acqua Felice. Axis c. 110/290; 565 m after Elagabalus shortened it (originally c. 630 m).

sette_sale.note: OSM outline; straight W facade with niches (rot 271), curved E side buried in the slope. Its orientation differs from the Baths of Trajan.

arch_of_constantine.note: OSM outline 25.4 x 7.0 m, facade line 103/283; faces NNE toward the Meta Sudans and Colosseum (rot 13) and SSW toward Via di S. Gregorio.

temple_castor_v2.summary: L. Caecilius Metellus Dalmaticus rebuilt the temple in 117 BC after his Dalmatian triumph on a high podium with a speakers' tribunal in its front, used in the political battles of the late Republic; Verres' notorious contract for its columns (74 BC) is the subject of a speech of Cicero.
